description: A low-resource Windows browser shell built on WebView2, whose core bet is that hibernated is a tab's default state and live is a budgeted exception.
consumer_notes: This file is the authoritative machine-readable model of WHY this codebase is shaped the way it is. Source code records what the system does; this graph records the reasoning, the rejected alternatives, and the constraints that must not be violated. Agents should read this before proposing architectural changes. Every node has a stable `id` that is safe to reference in commits, issues, and other documents. When you add a feature, add its nodes/edges here in the same commit.

node_types.api: An external platform API the design depends on.

node_types.commit: A unit of work in this repository's history.

nodes.label: Users hoard tabs and will not close them
nodes.summary: People keep 100-500 tabs open because the tab strip is the only place where 'things I still care about' remain visible. Refusing to close is a rational response to untrustworthy retrieval, not user error.

nodes.label: The RAM cost of tabs is invisible to users
nodes.summary: Users experience the symptom (a slow machine) but do not attribute it to the browser. Because the cost is never made legible, there is no pressure to change behaviour.

nodes.label: Existing tab suspenders restore lossily
nodes.summary: Chrome Memory Saver, The Great Suspender and similar tools lose scroll position, form state and media timestamps on restore. The papercut causes users to disable the feature, so the memory is never actually reclaimed.

nodes.label: Tab archivers become graveyards
nodes.summary: OneTab, Session Buddy and Toby convert a visible anxious pile into an invisible list nobody revisits. Users intuit this and resist adoption, correctly.

nodes.label: Per-renderer baseline dominates browser memory
nodes.summary: A Chromium renderer costs roughly 40-80 MB for a blank page (V8 isolate, Blink, Mojo, sandbox) before any content loads. At 100 tabs that is ~6 GB of pure overhead. Tab COUNT, not page weight, is the primary cost driver.
nodes.implication: Any memory strategy that does not reduce the number of live renderers is treating a symptom.

nodes.label: A tab strip holds five different data types
nodes.summary: Active work, a todo, a reference doc, a read-later item, and a fear-of-loss artifact all wear the same UI costume. Applying one lifecycle policy to all five is why every existing tool fails.

nodes.label: Refindability score
nodes.summary: How hard a tab would be to recover if closed. A homepage or Wikipedia article is trivially refindable; a filtered dashboard view, a deep search result, or a half-filled form is not. Aggressive eviction is acceptable only for trivially refindable tabs.

nodes.label: Trade RAM for disk at ~200:1
nodes.summary: A hibernated tab costs a WebP screenshot plus serialised state, roughly 150 KB on disk, versus 40-80 MB of RAM live. 200 hibernated tabs fit in ~40 MB of disk.

nodes.label: Hibernated is the default state, live is the exception
nodes.summary: Every other browser treats loaded as default and unloading as an emergency. Chrome Memory Saver and Firefox tab unloading are REACTIVE, triggering only under memory pressure. Hearth inverts this: tabs are documents on disk that get temporarily instantiated, under a hard budget.

nodes.label: Build a shell on WebView2 rather than fork an engine
nodes.summary: WebView2 provides the modern web for free and natively exposes the exact primitives this architecture needs: TrySuspend/Resume, CapturePreview, and MemoryUsageTargetLevel. A Gecko fork would give deeper process-model control but costs months before the UX thesis can be tested at all.
nodes.rationale: De-risk the product thesis on the cheap substrate first. If screenshot-backed restore does not feel convincing here, a Gecko fork inherits the same failure.
nodes.revisit_if: Shell-level control proves insufficient to hold a hard memory ceiling, or cross-platform support becomes a requirement.

nodes.label: C# / .NET 9 / WPF as the host framework
nodes.summary: WPF is the most mature WebView2 host, builds from the CLI without MSIX packaging friction, and allows direct control over individual CoreWebView2Controller lifetimes.
nodes.rationale: Chosen partly by environment: .NET 9 SDK and VS 2022 present, no Rust toolchain installed. WinUI3 was rejected for packaging friction.

nodes.label: One shared CoreWebView2Environment for all tabs
nodes.summary: Every WebView2 created from a single environment shares ONE browser process. Allowing each control to create its own environment (the default) spawns a browser process per tab and destroys the memory budget before it exists.
nodes.rationale: This is the single highest-leverage line of code in the project.
nodes.invariant: Never call EnsureCoreWebView2Async without passing the shared environment.

nodes.label: No per-tab memory API is exposed
nodes.summary: Neither WebView2 nor Chromium exposes per-renderer memory to embedders. Per-tab cost must be inferred by measuring the reclaim delta across a suspend/resume cycle, or by attributing OS process working sets.
nodes.workaround: Measure system-wide working set of the WebView2 process tree before and after eviction; attribute the delta to the evicted tab. Self-calibrating over time.

nodes.label: Widevine DRM requires a licence agreement
nodes.summary: Netflix, Spotify and Prime need Widevine. WebView2 inherits Edge's Widevine support, but a shipped product needs a licence relationship with Google. Not a coding problem.

nodes.label: WebView2 is Windows-only in practice
nodes.summary: WebView2 targets Windows. Cross-platform would require CEF, Tauri's wry, or a per-OS webview abstraction.

nodes.label: CapturePreview requires a live, realised WebView2
nodes.summary: A screenshot can only be taken while the WebView2 still exists and has rendered. The capture must therefore happen at tab-BLUR, immediately before eviction, never after.
nodes.implication: A tab restored from a cold session has no screenshot until it has been live once.

nodes.label: Renderer count exceeds tab count because of site isolation
nodes.summary: WebView2 inherits Chromium site isolation, which allocates a renderer per site instance INCLUDING cross-origin iframes. Measured at commit 0002: 5 tabs (example.com, wikipedia, HN, github, stackoverflow) produced 14 renderer processes and 1170 MB total working set, roughly 234 MB per tab.
nodes.implication: A shared environment guarantees one BROWSER process, not one renderer per tab. Capping live tabs alone does not cap renderers; ad-heavy or widget-heavy pages fan out. This makes eviction MORE valuable than the original 40-80 MB per-tab estimate implied, not less.
nodes.known_lever: CoreWebView2EnvironmentOptions.AdditionalBrowserArguments can pass --renderer-process-limit=N, which forces Chromium to multiplex site instances onto a capped renderer pool, in the spirit of Firefox's dom.ipc.processCount. Untested here as of 0002; evaluated in 0003.
nodes.tradeoff: Capping renderers weakens site isolation, the mitigation for Spectre-class cross-origin attacks, and makes one renderer crash take down more tabs.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2EnvironmentOptions.AdditionalBrowserArguments
nodes.summary: Passes raw Chromium command-line switches to the browser process at environment-creation time. The only route to process-model control from an embedder, and therefore the only lever on k.site-isolation-multiplies-renderers.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.TrySuspend()
nodes.summary: Suspends a WebView2, freeing significant renderer memory while keeping the controller alive for fast resume. Requires the controller to be invisible first. This is hibernation tier 1.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.CapturePreviewAsync()
nodes.summary: Captures the visible content of a WebView2 to a PNG or JPEG stream. Used to produce the visual placeholder that makes an evicted tab indistinguishable from a live one.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.MemoryUsageTargetLevel
nodes.summary: Hints to the runtime that a WebView2 should minimise memory usage. Cheaper and lower-fidelity than TrySuspend; usable as an intermediate tier for recently-blurred tabs.

nodes.label: Steady-state working set at high tab count
nodes.summary: Target: total working set stays flat as tab count grows. Reference points: Chrome at 100 tabs is 6-10 GB, Firefox 2-4 GB. Hearth target is under 1.5 GB regardless of tab count.

baseline_0002.note: Measured BEFORE any budget or eviction exists. This is the number the project has to beat, not a result.
baseline_0002.interpretation: Growth is roughly linear and steep. Naive linear extrapolation to 100 tabs is over 20 GB, i.e. currently WORSE than Chrome. The entire value of the project is in flattening this curve.

nodes.label: Restore fidelity
nodes.summary: Whether a rehydrated tab returns to the same scroll offset, form state and media position. The product thesis fails if users can feel eviction happening.

nodes.label: Memory reclaimed per eviction
nodes.summary: Working-set bytes returned to the OS by evicting one tab. Doubles as the per-tab cost estimate that makes the invisible cost legible to users.

nodes.label: App / StoreRoot
nodes.summary: Application entry point. Owns StoreRoot, the single on-disk location for the WebView2 user-data folder, hibernation screenshots and the session index.

nodes.label: MainWindow
nodes.summary: Application shell. At commit 0001 it hosts a single WebView2 and creates the shared environment, proving the toolchain. Becomes the tab-strip host in later commits.

nodes.label: TabState
nodes.summary: Four-state lifecycle enum (Live, Warm, Hibernated, Cold). Ordered so that a higher value means cheaper to hold and slower to restore; eviction always moves a tab to a higher value.

nodes.label: BrowserTab
nodes.summary: A tab's durable identity: URL, title, activation history. Deliberately NOT a WebView2 wrapper — the View property is nullable and null is the expected steady state. Carries LastActivatedUtc and ActivationCount to drive eviction ordering.
nodes.invariant: Null View must never be treated as an error condition. Tabs are documents; renderers are a cache.

nodes.label: TabManager
nodes.summary: Owns tab lifetime and the single shared CoreWebView2Environment. Holds the environment as a Task awaited by every realisation, so tabs share one initialisation instead of racing to create their own.
nodes.invariant: RealiseAsync is the ONLY place permitted to call EnsureCoreWebView2Async, and it always passes the shared environment.

nodes.label: 0001 - scaffold
nodes.summary: Repo initialised, WPF + WebView2 shell builds and navigates, documentation and knowledge-graph structure established.

nodes.label: 0002 - tab model
nodes.summary: Tab abstraction and TabManager introduced; environment ownership moved out of the window. Verified one browser process across 5 tabs, and discovered site isolation multiplies renderers well beyond tab count.

edges.note: Users resist archiving precisely because archives are not trustworthy retrieval.
Eviction is only acceptable if restore is indistinguishable from never having left.
Supersedes MainWindow as the environment owner.
For environment ownership only; MainWindow remains the shell.
Nullable View encodes 'a tab is a document, a renderer is a cache'.
A shared environment guarantees one BROWSER process, not one renderer per tab.
